title: How do you trace a request across service boundaries?
description: Correlation ids, spans, and OpenTelemetry: stitching sync calls, async events, and logs into one end-to-end view of a request.

data.text: **Question:** How do you trace a request across service boundaries?

With **distributed tracing**: the entry point generates a **trace id**, and every service hop creates **spans** (one timed operation each) that carry the trace context forward via headers (W3C `traceparent`) or event metadata. **OpenTelemetry** is the standard: SDK + API instrument once, export to a backend (Jaeger, Zipkin, Azure Monitor, Datadog, Tempo). The context must propagate across **HTTP calls, message queues, and background jobs** — the async boundaries are where traces normally break. Spans correlate with **structured logs** (trace id on every log line) and **metrics** (per-endpoint latency/error rates), forming the three pillars. In .NET: OpenTelemetry packages + `AddOpenTelemetry().WithTracing(...)` auto-instrument ASP.NET Core, HttpClient, and EF Core.

**The model:**
- **Trace**: the full journey of one request, identified by trace id
- **Span**: one unit of work (an HTTP call, a DB query, a queue publish) with start/end, status, and attributes (route, user id, row counts)
- **Parent-child links**: spans record their parent — the tree reconstructs causality, not just timing
- **Context propagation** is the whole game: outbound calls must inject trace context into headers (W3C Trace Context standard: `traceparent: 00-<trace-id>-<span-id>-01`); inbound calls extract it; queue consumers attach the producer's context to a new child span

**What good instrumentation captures:**
- Every outbound dependency call as a span — that's what shows '4.2s total, 3.9s in the payments dependency'
- Span attributes: http.route (not raw URLs — cardinality explosion), db.system, messaging.destination
- Errors on the span with status + exception, sampled attributes for filtering
- Baggage (key-value context) for cross-cutting values like tenant id

**Async boundaries:**
- Message producers: inject context into message headers/payload envelope
- Consumers: extract, start a child span — the trace continues across the queue
- Fire-and-forget/background jobs: start a new root span linked to the original (span links) — causality preserved even without a strict parent

**Sampling & cost:**
- Head-based sampling (decide at the root) controls volume; tail-based sampling (decide after, keep all errors/slows) gives better fidelity at higher cost
- Always keep error and high-latency traces; sample the happy path

**.NET concrete:** `builder.Services.AddOpenTelemetry().WithTracing(t => t.AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation().AddHttpClientInstrumentation().AddEntityFrameworkCoreInstrumentation())` + OTLP exporter; Serilog enrichers add TraceId/SpanId to every log line

data.title: Instrumenting a .NET service and carrying context across a queue
Traces answer 'why', metrics answer 'is it broken'
data.text: Metrics (p99 latency by endpoint, error rate) tell you something is wrong; the trace for one slow request tells you exactly which dependency, query, or lock caused it. Instrument both from day one — and put the trace id in your error pages/tickets so support can jump straight to the waterfall.

items: Tracing HTTP but not messaging — the trace dies at the queue, which is usually where the latency hides
High-cardinality attributes (raw URLs, user ids in metric names) — exploding backend costs
No sampling strategy — 100% of traces at full volume is a bill, not observability
Trace ids only in traces, not in logs — you can't pivot from an error log to the waterfall
Manual instrumentation everywhere when auto-instrumentation covers the framework stack
Forgetting background workers — they need ActivitySources too, or their latency is invisible

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Trace id at entry; every hop adds spans; headers/events carry the context
OpenTelemetry: instrument once, export anywhere; auto-instrument the framework stack
The hard part is propagation across queues and background jobs
Logs + metrics + traces stitched by ids = the full debugging story
data.takeaway: A request's story is only complete when context crosses every boundary you own — the queue, the job, the retry — or your traces will lie by omission.
